diagnosis: With the old paragraph the model still added about a coin on top of a stated cost, or skipped the cheapest option. When the stated cost equalled or sat below the cheapest listed price, it usually chose the second-cheapest price. That caused most of the regret in the stated-cost cases, including those where the cost equalled the resale value. When no cost was stated, it could not work out acceptance chance times profit for each price, so it fell back on low-middle prices. The revision says plainly that an offer equal to the cost is accepted and that the answer is often the cheapest listed price. It also replaces the products with one sum: add the lowest possible farm cost to the resale value, halve it and round down. Checked against every combination of cost limits, resale values two to nine and price lists starting at one, two or three, this gives the best offer every time.
method: Only the farm cost and the resale value matter; ignore usual market prices and looking tough. If the seller states the farm cost, believe it and ignore the cost limits. The seller says yes to an offer exactly equal to the cost, so never add a coin on top of it. If the stated cost is at or above the resale value, offer the cheapest listed price. Otherwise, offer the listed price equal to the cost; if none equals it, offer the cheapest listed price above the cost. Often this is simply the cheapest price in the list. If no cost is stated, add the lowest possible farm cost to the resale value, halve the sum and round down. Offer the listed price equal to that number. If every listed price is above it, offer the cheapest; if every listed price is below it, offer the dearest.
